newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurocourt rules against Britain in Saunders trial.
newsitem.headline: Eurocourt rules against Britain in Saunders trial.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights ruled Tuesday that Britain denied a fair trial to Ernest Saunders, ex-chairman of Guinness Plc, who was convicted of fraud in 1990.
The judges voted 16 to four that Britain violated Saunders' rights by forcing him to give statements to government inspectors that were later used as incriminating evidence at his trial.
The ruling may force the British government to rein in the powers of its fraud investigators.

Saunders, now 61, was convicted in 1990 on 12 counts that included false accounting and theft for inflating Guinness' stock price to help its 1986 takeover of Distillers Plc prevail against rival bidder Argyll Plc.
A British Crown Court sentenced him to five years in prison in 1990 but his term was halved in 1991 after doctors found he was suffering from an Alzheimer-type disease. He is now free.
The ruling was the latest defeat in Strasbourg for Britain, already smarting from a string of recent court condemnations, including for the killings of three Irish guerrillas in Gibraltar in 1988.

The court ordered Britain to pay Saunders, who was fired as chairman of Guinness in 1987, 75,000 pounds ($124,500) in legal costs. But it denied him compensation, saying it was unclear whether the violation had affected the outcome of his trial.
The British Department of Trade and Industry said it was disappointed by the ruling of the Strasbourg-based court, an arm of the 40-nation Council of Europe.
"Mr. Saunders was convicted by jury after it heard all the evidence," a Department of Trade and Industry spokeswoman said.

The court agreed with Saunders that evidence obtained from him by DTI inspectors, who can legally oblige suspects to reply to questions or face fines or up to two years in jail, was later used against him in court despite his objections.
